hints: Focus on what standard enthalpy of formation really means, forming exactly one mole of the compound from its elements.
Notice that sodium oxide is $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$, so you need 2 moles of $\text{Na(s)}$ and oxygen as $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$ to make just 1 mole of it.
Check each equation for exactly 1 mole of product with elements in their standard states, balancing with fractions if you need to.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of standard enthalpy of formation**

Standard enthalpy of formation, $\Delta H_f^\ominus$, is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states.

Definition rule:
$$1 \text{ mol compound formed from elements (standard states)}$$

**Apply it to sodium oxide**

The product must be exactly $1$ mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$. The elements are sodium as $\text{Na(s)}$ and oxygen as $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$.

Required equation form:
$$2\text{Na(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$$

**Match to the options**

Only one equation makes exactly one mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$ from $\text{Na(s)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$ with correct balancing. Fractions like $\tfrac{1}{2}$ are allowed to keep the product at 1 mole.

options.A: Forms only $\tfrac{1}{2}$ mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$, so its enthalpy change is $\tfrac{1}{2} \Delta H_f^\ominus$. The trap is thinking fractions are not allowed, but here the product amount is wrong.
options.B: Uses $1$ mole of $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$ for $1$ mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$, which is not balanced and gives excess oxygen. Formation must use exactly $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$ to make $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$.
options.C: Correctly forms exactly $1$ mole of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$ from $2\text{Na(s)}$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$ in their standard states. This matches the definition of $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ perfectly.
options.D: Forms $2$ moles of $\text{Na}_2\text{O(s)}$, so its enthalpy change is $2 \times \Delta H_f^\ominus$. The trap is choosing a fully balanced equation with whole numbers but forgetting the product must be 1 mole.
